Cada clave RSA, cada primo de Diffie-Hel: Every RSA key, every Diffie-Hellman prime and every elliptic curve that is generated goes through this test, and cryptographic libraries run it millions of times a day. It is also an example of an idea that goes beyond primes: a probabilistic algorithm that is wrong with controlled probability can be much better than an exact but unusable one, and in many computing problems that is today the only way forward.

Comprobar si un número de 300 cifras es: Checking whether a 300-digit number is prime by dividing it is not possible: divisors up to $10^{150}$ would have to be tried. And yet your phone generates two such primes every time it creates a key. It does so with a test that does not prove a number is prime, but stops doubting it with an error probability that can be made as small as you like, and that is smaller than the chance of the computer getting an addition wrong.

El pequeño teorema de Fermat dice que si: Fermat's little theorem says that if $n$ is prime, $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $a$ that is not a multiple of $n$. Turning it round: if for some $a$ something else comes out, $n$ is certainly not prime. That $a$ is called a witness. And computing $a^{n-1} \bmod n$ costs a few hundred multiplications by successive squaring.
El problema es el recíproco. Si sale 1,: The problem is the converse. If 1 comes out, $n$ might be prime. For most composites, almost any base gives them away. But there is a family, the Carmichael numbers, that satisfy $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$ for every base sharing no factor with them: 561, 1105, 1729… There are infinitely many, and Fermat's test does not tell them apart from primes.

Fermat enunció su pequeño teorema en una: Fermat stated his little theorem in a letter of 1640, with no proof, and Euler proved it in 1736. Robert Carmichael found in 1910 the numbers that fool Fermat, and it was proved in 1994 that there are infinitely many. Gary Miller published in 1976 a deterministic test that depended on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and Michael Rabin turned it in 1980 into the probabilistic test used ever since. In 2002, Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena, two of them students, gave the first deterministic polynomial-time test with no hypotheses; it was news all over the world, and it replaced Miller-Rabin nowhere.

La mejora es exigir más. Si $n$ es primo: The improvement is to demand more. If $n$ is prime, the only square roots of 1 modulo $n$ are $1$ and $-1$. You write $n - 1 = 2^s d$ with $d$ odd, and look at the sequence $a^d, a^{2d}, a^{4d}, \dots, a^{2^{s-1}d}$, each term the square of the previous one. If $n$ is prime, either $a^d \equiv 1$, or some term of the sequence is $-1$. If neither happens, $n$ is composite and $a$ is a witness.
